symptom: `mxcli check`/`exec` reports **MDL041** "assigning a Decimal expression to Integer variable" on arithmetic that mxbuild builds at **0 errors** — `round(floor($a div 3)) * 3` is refused while the same expression without the `* 3` is accepted. Since `exec` refuses to write when any rule errors, the model's own `describe` output cannot be fed back to `exec`, and anything built on that round trip (mutation harnesses, generators) silently applies nothing
cause: `round`/`floor`/`ceil` were declared `ret: KindDecimal` in `funcTable` and exempted from the check only when the call was the WHOLE right-hand side. As soon as the rounded value became an operand, the inner `div`'s Decimal taint propagated back out through the very function that exists to stop it. The same root-only shortcut let the genuinely Decimal two-argument `round($a div $b, 2)` through, and `abs`/`max`/`min` — which preserve their operands' kind — were false positives on every Integer argument
file: `mdl/exprcheck/func_checker.go` (`funcSig.retByArity`/`retFromArgs`/`retFor`, the Math table), `mdl/exprcheck/parser.go` (`inferKind` CallExpr arm, `callArgsResult`), `mdl/exprcheck/unknown_funcs.go` (`SourceRejectedForIntegerTarget`; `roundingFuncs` deleted); test `mdl/exprcheck/round_returns_integer_test.go`; repro `mdl-examples/bug-tests/sudoku-49-mdl041-rounding-arithmetic.mdl`
insight: Give the function table a return kind that is right at **every** call site instead of exempting a name at the root: arity-dependent for `round` (1 arg Integer, 2 args Decimal), Integer for `floor`/`ceil`, operand-derived for `abs`/`max`/`min`. Then the rule just asks `inferKind`, and `arithResult` propagates it through the surrounding arithmetic for free. **Measure the table against mxbuild, one row at a time** — `mxcli exec --no-check` writes the expression, `mx check` judges it — and include the bare `$a div 3` control, or a table of "0 errors" proves only that the validator never fires. Cheaper alternative deliberately NOT taken: downgrading MDL041 to a warning so it cannot block `exec`. **The generalisable trap: making a checker authoritative (refuse-before-write) turns every false positive from an annoyance into a blocked workflow** — the rules behind such a gate have to be at least as accurate as the tool they are protecting you from, and this one was measurably less accurate than `mx check` on 10 of 18 probes.
